text: Left to its own defaults, every Windows machine checks in with Microsoft directly and installs updates on its own schedule. At home, that's fine. Across a company with a thousand machines, it wastes bandwidth as every machine separately re-downloads the same multi-gigabyte update, and it gives IT zero control over which updates go out and when. Windows offers two real, different fixes: WSUS and Windows Update for Business.

Windows Server Update Services, WSUS, is a server role. It downloads updates from Microsoft once, and every other machine checks that server instead of the internet. The real value isn't bandwidth, though — it's control. Nothing reaches a client automatically: an administrator reviews each update and explicitly approves or declines it, then targets approved updates to computer groups like Pilot Ring or Finance Workstations, staggering the rollout the tool itself is built around.

Windows Update for Business takes a different approach. There's no on-premises server to install or maintain. Instead, behavior is set through policy — Group Policy, or more commonly Intune — using deployment rings and deferral periods. A Pilot ring might receive updates immediately, while a Broad ring is configured with a 14-day deferral, so those updates simply don't install until the pilot ring has had time to surface problems first.

WSUS fits a traditional, on-premises Active Directory environment where IT already runs its own servers and wants update-by-update control. WUfB fits a cloud-managed fleet — laptops enrolled in Intune, often remote, that may rarely touch the corporate network, where standing up a WSUS server is extra infrastructure for little benefit. Plenty of real organizations run both at once, deliberately, during a multi-year move from on-premises AD to cloud-managed Intune.

Those are the two real ways Windows handles patching at scale. Linux splits along a different line entirely: which package-manager family a distribution belongs to. Next, the real apt workflow on Debian and Ubuntu, and the real yum and dnf workflow on the Red Hat family.
